turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on back, I'll get your numbers before he calls you. Left arm up on the rest, please.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure, I always give them the left because the right one has a little scar from an IV years ago, and the cuff pinches it, which is probably nothing but I mention it every time anyway.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): First read was one fifty-six over ninety-four, but the cuff was crooked. Recheck is one forty-eight over ninety-two.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): My home machine said something like one fifty after dinner last night, though the batteries are ancient so I don't really trust that thing, and I know after dinner is a silly time to check.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse seventy-eight. Oxygen is ninety-eight percent. Respirations sixteen. He'll be in shortly.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll sit in, if that's okay. I keep his pill box and I drove, so I catch the things he talks past.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): She lives in the spare room, has since my wife passed, and it just works better that way. I do remember my own medicines, I just take the scenic route explaining them.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this screen froze on me again. Alright. What got you in today?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this cough. Dry, nothing comes up. It's been two weeks, well actually if I count it right it's been five weeks. I kept blaming a cold.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Five weeks, dry. Say that once more, I was clicking and I only half heard you.

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Five weeks, dry cough, a tickle right in the throat. At night it comes in spells, every few minutes for about an hour, worse lying down, and worse if I talk a long time. Sips of water help, and two pillows help some. I figured the cold's runny nose is what kicked it off.
[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm sorry, it's not five. I wrote it on the calendar. He's been coughing eight weeks.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't buy eight. The cold was around then, and I tied the cough to that cold the whole time, which may be me being stubborn.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hold on, it logged me out. So call it somewhere between five and eight weeks, I'm not getting you two to agree. The runny nose, is that gone?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Gone. The stuffy nose cleared up too. Cough stuck around. No fever, I checked a few mornings with the old thermometer.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any phlegm? Any wheezing?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No phlegm at all. I don't wheeze. And I don't get short of breath, I can walk the block just fine.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. Meds next, this list is a mess. What are you actually taking?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine five milligrams every morning, for five-ish years, for the blood pressure, that one never changes. They added enalapril, no, wait, it's ramipril. I mix them up because my sister takes lisinopril.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ramipril, not enalapril. I typed the wrong one. What dose, one more time?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I was going to say ten milligrams, but the bottle is five milligrams, once a day, for my high blood pressure. I started it recently, three weeks ago or a month, I cannot tell you the day.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The start date is fuzzy for me too. What I do know is the ramipril is still sitting there two or three mornings a week. He walks out without taking it.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): That isn't really fair. I take it every day. There was one morning the plumber was over and I might have forgotten, but I am not skipping it all the time.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): So it's prescribed once a day, and whether every dose happens is a little murky. I'm still scrolling. Anything else in the box?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): A cholesterol pill, for my high cholesterol. Small white oval, at bedtime. I think maybe twenty milligrams, I'm not sure of that number. The name has completely left me, something that might start with an A, or maybe it doesn't.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the bottle isn't here we'll leave the name. This screen jumped again. Any swelling in the legs? Any chest pain?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. No chest pain. Nothing squeezing or heavy, I would have led with that, I really would.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me listen. Big breaths.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear, no wheeze. Heart is regular, I don't hear a murmur. Throat's a little pink, nothing dramatic.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): The pink is from coughing all evening, I bet. And I need to take back what I said. On the stairs up to the spare room I do get winded, and a long story does it too. Not while I'm just sitting.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He stops halfway up those stairs and holds the rail. He usually won't say so.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Short of breath on stairs and with talking, not at rest. I need you to repeat the night part, I was typing.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Lying down it picks up. Two pillows, sips of water. I don't wake up gasping. It eases if I sit up.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Phone calls with his sister set it off too. Those go on forever.

[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud, so don't file this as a diagnosis. Dry cough for weeks after a cold, and ramipril got started somewhere in that same stretch. That drug can cause a cough. A cold can leave one too. I am not saying which this is.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister coughed on lisinopril and they changed hers, that's the only reason I thought of it. She has high blood pressure, and our dad had it as well. I don't want to just borrow her story and slap it on me.

[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not diagnosing the cough today. I do want you off the ramipril. We'll use losartan instead, twenty-five, no, fifty milligrams, once a day, by mouth, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty, once a day, in place of the five of ramipril. Do I start tonight or in the morning? And the amlodipine stays? The white cholesterol one too?

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine stays, five milligrams every morning. Keep the cholesterol pill the way you have been until we can read the name. Start losartan tomorrow morning. Do not take the ramipril anymore, starting now.
[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll take the ramipril out of the box tonight so it doesn't sneak back in. The colors are close and he rushes in the morning.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril is the little capsule, not the tablet, that's how I tell them, when I tell them. Is there a real chance this is just the cold and I'm switching for nothing?

[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's still open. Could be the ramipril, could be the tail of the cold. Your pressure is still up a bit, and losartan is a solid substitute, so the switch makes sense either way. If the drug is the cause, the cough can take weeks to fade, and I am not calling it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it doesn't fade? I'd rather not collect tests. I had my appendix out as a kid and I still get sour just walking into a hospital, which is off the point, I know.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): If it's not settling in about three weeks, then we can get a chest x-ray. I'm not ordering that today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I come back even if I feel okay? My Tuesdays are usually the block walk and the grocery, so a morning visit is easier than afternoon, if you care about that.

[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in three weeks either way. We'll recheck the pressure and the cough. Sooner, don't wait, if your lips or face swell, or if you can't catch your breath while you're resting.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Three weeks, on the fridge. I'm writing fifty milligrams, not the twenty-five you said first.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fifty. I corrected that. Ramipril is finished. Can you say the plan back? I was in the order screen and I want to be sure it landed.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop ramipril now, losartan fifty milligrams tomorrow morning, amlodipine five stays. I still walk the block most days, unless the cough makes me self-conscious. I don't smoke, never have. I stopped drinking about ten years ago, and it wasn't much even then.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Walking is fine, just ease off if you get winded. Pillows and sips of water like you've been doing. I don't need you on a cough syrup.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): The after-visit print is stuck behind the same frozen window. Did you want any labs? Nothing is on my list.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): No labs today. Just the medicine change.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): One more cough detail, because I time things. At night it comes in spells, maybe every few minutes for an hour, and then it backs off. It is not the entire night.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say the spell part again. A message popped up over the note.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Spells at night, every few minutes or so, for about an hour, then quieter. Not constant.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any weight change? Feeling cold?
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): No, weight's the same. I'm not feeling cold. Appetite's fine. I was about to tell you about the neighbor's dog and it has zero to do with this, so I won't.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He eats what I cook, normal portions. I haven't seen any weight loss.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then the plan stands. Stop ramipril, start losartan fifty milligrams tomorrow morning, amlodipine unchanged, see me in three weeks. On the cough, no firm cause today.
[SEG0060] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And swelling of the lips means we don't sit on it until that visit.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Emergency care for lip or face swelling, or if he is short of breath just sitting still.

[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll bring the cholesterol bottle next time. The label is half rubbed off, which is my fault, I keep it in a cup by the sink, but you can probably still read the name off what's left.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): Please bring it. That name is still up in the air.
[SEG0064] person_1 (NURSE): Vitals are filed, including the recheck, one forty-eight over ninety-two. You can head to the desk whenever you're done talking.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one forty-eight something I should panic about? I spiral on numbers, I check them, I recheck them, and then I explain them to whoever is standing there.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's a bit high, which is why we keep treating it. Not an emergency today.
[SEG0067] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Those home-cuff batteries, should I just replace them? He argues with the machine every evening.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): New batteries are fine. Don't chase the number all day.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): I usually check after the late news, which is a terrible habit, and the news itself is grim enough without a cuff squeezing me.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): If you check at all, once a day is enough, around the same time.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning, then. Before the pills or after the amlodipine? I can overthink a glass of water, so I'm asking plain.
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): Before the morning pills, sitting quietly, if you want a home reading. It's optional.
[SEG0073] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll set out the losartan tomorrow and I'll toss the ramipril tonight. I don't want both white things in the same slot.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): Please don't toss the amlodipine. Ramipril is the capsule. Amlodipine is a tablet. I know I said the colors are close, that's why I'm repeating it.
[SEG0075] person_4 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine stays. Only ramipril goes. Losartan is the new tablet, fifty milligrams.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Got it. Five milligrams of amlodipine, fifty of losartan, and no more of the five milligram ramipril. I'll stop talking before I add a footnote.
[SEG0077] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you toward the desk when you're ready. No bloodwork slip from me.
[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): See you in three weeks. We'll just watch the cough until then.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Bedtime cholesterol pill is supported; 20 mg is uncertain, not established.
bad.text: small white oval pill for cholesterol (dose=20 mg, frequency=at bedtime, indication=high cholesterol, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Initial blood pressure reading was 156/94 before repeat measurement; cuff was crooked on the first reading.
Patient reported a home blood pressure reading around 150 after dinner the night before, though he did not trust the machine because the batteries were old.
Negative finding: patient denied shortness of breath initially, saying he could walk the block fine, before later clarifying he does get winded on stairs and with prolonged talking.
Medication detail recorded incorrectly: the cholesterol pill dose was uncertain ('I think maybe 20 mg, I'm not sure'), not a confirmed 20 mg dose.
Doctor explicitly said no labs today.
